---
title: "References"
subtitle: "Readings by module, the courses and documentation this workshop draws on, and how each entry was checked"
---

Every lecture page ends with five readings and a note on why each matters. This page collects them, together with the other works the lectures cite, as full citations with stable links. A source appears in full once, under the first module that lists it as a reading; later modules point back to it.

## How the entries were checked

Each entry ends with a note in italics saying how its citation was checked on 2026-10-05:

- **Verified** (with the source): the authors, title, year, venue and pages match a primary or authoritative record that we opened. These records are the ACL Anthology's own metadata files, the metadata files of the Proceedings of Machine Learning Research (PMLR), PyPI, a project's own repository, or the documentation page itself.
- **Search summary**: the details match several independent web search results, but we could not open the publisher's page. The build environment cannot reach arXiv, the ACL Anthology website, the NeurIPS, ICLR and OpenReview proceedings, or most publishers.
- **Not read**: the source exists, but no one writing the workshop has read it from the build environment. The entry says what is missing.

No entry is cited from memory alone. Page ranges and DOIs are given only where a check confirmed them.

## Courses

- Stanford University. [CS224N: Natural Language Processing with Deep Learning](https://web.stanford.edu/class/cs224n/). The model for this workshop's order of ideas: derive, implement, then use the library. *Search summary.*
- Carnegie Mellon University. [CS 11-747: Neural Networks for NLP](https://phontron.com/class/nn4nlp2021/), Graham Neubig, 2021 edition. The model for code-first lectures in which every equation maps to code. *Search summary.*
- Massachusetts Institute of Technology. [6.S191: Introduction to Deep Learning](https://introtodeeplearning.com/), Alexander Amini and Ava Amini. The model for short lectures followed at once by a lab. *Search summary.*

## Textbooks

- Jurafsky, D. and Martin, J. H. [*Speech and Language Processing*](https://web.stanford.edu/~jurafsky/slp3/), 3rd edition draft (the August 2026 release). Free chapter PDFs. Chapter numbers change between draft releases, so the lectures name chapters by title. Modules 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6 use the chapters "Words and Tokens", "N-gram Language Models", "Logistic Regression and Text Classification", "Embeddings", "Neural Networks", "RNNs and LSTMs", "Transformers and Pretraining" and "Masked Language Models". *Search summary: the draft and its August 2026 release confirmed; the chapter titles were not checked against the current table of contents.*

## Day 1 · Foundations

### Module 1 · Text as data

- Manning, C. D., Raghavan, P. and Schütze, H. (2008). [*Introduction to Information Retrieval*](https://nlp.stanford.edu/IR-book/). Cambridge University Press. Chapter 6 (term weighting and TF-IDF), chapter 13 (text classification and naive Bayes), and section 11.4.3, "Okapi BM25: a non-binary model", for the BM25 stretch exercise of Lab 1. *Search summary.*
- Chen, S. F. and Goodman, J. (1999). An empirical study of smoothing techniques for language modeling. *Computer Speech & Language* 13(4), 359–394. The standard comparison of smoothing methods, for the optional box on interpolation, backoff and Kneser–Ney. An earlier version appeared at ACL 1996: [An Empirical Study of Smoothing Techniques for Language Modeling](https://aclanthology.org/P96-1041/), *Proceedings of the 34th Annual Meeting of the ACL*, 310–318 (preprint [arXiv:cmp-lg/9606011](https://arxiv.org/abs/cmp-lg/9606011)). *Journal version: search summary. ACL 1996 version: verified, ACL Anthology.*
- Wang, S. and Manning, C. (2012). [Baselines and Bigrams: Simple, Good Sentiment and Topic Classification](https://aclanthology.org/P12-2018/). *Proceedings of the 50th Annual Meeting of the ACL (Volume 2: Short Papers)*, 90–94. Why a well-tuned linear model is a serious baseline. *Verified, ACL Anthology.*
- Robertson, S. E. and Zaragoza, H. (2009). [The Probabilistic Relevance Framework: BM25 and Beyond](https://doi.org/10.1561/1500000019). *Foundations and Trends in Information Retrieval* 3(4), 333–389. The derivation of BM25; also used in Module 13. *Search summary.*
- Also used: Jurafsky and Martin, the chapters "Words and Tokens", "N-gram Language Models" and "Logistic Regression and Text Classification" (Textbooks).

### Module 2 · Word vectors and neural networks

- Mikolov, T., Sutskever, I., Chen, K., Corrado, G. S. and Dean, J. (2013). [Distributed Representations of Words and Phrases and their Compositionality](https://arxiv.org/abs/1310.4546). *Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 26 (NIPS 2013)*, 3111–3119. Skip-gram with negative sampling, the loss implemented in Lab 2. *Search summary.*
- Goldberg, Y. and Levy, O. (2014). [word2vec Explained: deriving Mikolov et al.'s negative-sampling word-embedding method](https://arxiv.org/abs/1402.3722). arXiv:1402.3722. A slower version of the lecture's derivation. *Search summary.*
- Pennington, J., Socher, R. and Manning, C. (2014). [GloVe: Global Vectors for Word Representation](https://aclanthology.org/D14-1162/). *Proceedings of the 2014 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP)*, 1532–1543. *Verified, ACL Anthology.*
- Bengio, Y., Ducharme, R., Vincent, P. and Jauvin, C. (2003). [A Neural Probabilistic Language Model](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v3/bengio03a.html). *Journal of Machine Learning Research* 3, 1137–1155. The bridge from n-grams to neural language models. *Search summary.*
- Mikolov, T., Chen, K., Corrado, G. and Dean, J. (2013). [Efficient Estimation of Word Representations in Vector Space](https://arxiv.org/abs/1301.3781). arXiv:1301.3781. Skip-gram and CBOW. *Search summary.*
- Levy, O. and Goldberg, Y. (2014). [Neural Word Embedding as Implicit Matrix Factorization](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2014/hash/b78666971ceae55a8e87efb7cbfd9ad4-Abstract.html). *Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 27 (NIPS 2014)*. Skip-gram with negative sampling as a factorization of a shifted PMI matrix. *Search summary.*
- Levy, O., Goldberg, Y. and Dagan, I. (2015). [Improving Distributional Similarity with Lessons Learned from Word Embeddings](https://aclanthology.org/Q15-1016/). *Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics* 3, 211–225. *Verified, ACL Anthology.*
- Harris, Z. S. (1954). [Distributional Structure](https://doi.org/10.1080/00437956.1954.11659520). *Word* 10(2–3), 146–162. The distributional hypothesis. *Search summary.*
- Firth, J. R. (1957). A Synopsis of Linguistic Theory, 1930–1955. In *Studies in Linguistic Analysis* (special volume of the Philological Society), 1–32. Oxford: Blackwell. *Search summary; no stable link checked.*
- Also used: Jurafsky and Martin, the chapters "Embeddings" and "Neural Networks" (Textbooks).

### Module 3 · Sequence models

- Hochreiter, S. and Schmidhuber, J. (1997). [Long Short-Term Memory](https://doi.org/10.1162/neco.1997.9.8.1735). *Neural Computation* 9(8), 1735–1780. *Search summary.*
- Pascanu, R., Mikolov, T. and Bengio, Y. (2013). [On the difficulty of training recurrent neural networks](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v28/pascanu13.html). *Proceedings of the 30th International Conference on Machine Learning*, PMLR 28(3), 1310–1318. - Karpathy, A. (2015). [The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Recurrent Neural Networks](https://karpathy.github.io/2015/05/21/rnn-effectiveness/). Blog post, May 21, 2015. Character-level models on Shakespeare, the model for Lab 3. *Search summary.*
- Olah, C. (2015). [Understanding LSTM Networks](https://colah.github.io/posts/2015-08-Understanding-LSTMs/). Blog post, August 27, 2015. *Search summary.*
- Holtzman, A., Buys, J., Du, L., Forbes, M. and Choi, Y. (2020). [The Curious Case of Neural Text Degeneration](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.09751). *International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR 2020)*. Nucleus sampling, for the Lab 3 stretch section. *Search summary.*

- Also used: Cho et al. (2014), the GRU (Module 4).

### Module 4 · Seq2seq and attention

- Sutskever, I., Vinyals, O. and Le, Q. V. (2014). [Sequence to Sequence Learning with Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.3215). *Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 27 (NIPS 2014)*, 3104–3112. The LSTM encoder–decoder. *Search summary.*
- Bahdanau, D., Cho, K. and Bengio, Y. (2015). [Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.0473). *International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR 2015)*. The bottleneck and additive attention. *Search summary.*
- Luong, T., Pham, H. and Manning, C. D. (2015). [Effective Approaches to Attention-based Neural Machine Translation](https://aclanthology.org/D15-1166/). *Proceedings of the 2015 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing*, 1412–1421. Dot-product and general scores. *Verified, ACL Anthology.*
- Cho, K., van Merriënboer, B., Gulcehre, C., Bahdanau, D., Bougares, F., Schwenk, H. and Bengio, Y. (2014). [Learning Phrase Representations using RNN Encoder–Decoder for Statistical Machine Translation](https://aclanthology.org/D14-1179/). *Proceedings of the 2014 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP)*, 1724–1734. The RNN encoder–decoder and the GRU; also cited in Module 3. *Verified, ACL Anthology.*
- Also used: Jurafsky and Martin, the chapter "RNNs and LSTMs" (Textbooks).

## TypeSafe and Jev: public sources

TypeSafe has not published how RLCD works: we have found no paper, reward function or reliability data from TypeSafe. The only statement about training we found in TypeSafe's own material is "System One models are trained for calibrated decisions; validate their performance in the target domain." (`SKILL.md`, below). Lecture 12 separates what TypeSafe states from our illustration, and lists third-party reports about RLCD as unverified; those third-party pages are not TypeSafe sources and are not listed here.

- TypeSafe AI. [`typesafe-sdk`](https://pypi.org/project/typesafe-sdk/) 0.7.2, the Python SDK for Jev (MIT license; import name `typesafe_sdk`). Used in Labs 12 to 14. *Verified, PyPI.*
- TypeSafe AI. [`typesafe-ai/skills`](https://github.com/typesafe-ai/skills), the file `skills/typesafe-ai/SKILL.md`: TypeSafe's guidance on typed questions, probabilities and `confidence`, and the training sentence quoted above. *Verified, GitHub repository.*
- TypeSafe AI. [`system-one-adapter`](https://pypi.org/project/system-one-adapter/) 0.2.1, a drop-in replacement for the SDK client backed by LLM APIs, for comparing the two. *Verified, PyPI.*
- TypeSafe AI. [`WorkflowEvals`](https://github.com/typesafe-ai/WorkflowEvals), the code behind TypeSafe's published workflow evaluations. *Verified, GitHub repository.*
- [`langchain-typesafe`](https://pypi.org/project/langchain-typesafe/) 0.0.1a3, a LangChain integration for TypeSafe classifiers (a pre-release version). Used in Lab 14. *Verified, PyPI.*
- TypeSafe AI. `docs.typesafe.ai` (overview, the confidence page, the Python SDK page) and TypeSafe's Jev announcement. *Not read: the build environment could not reach them. TypeSafe's own repository links to `docs.typesafe.ai`. Lecture 12 carries a TODO to quote them before the module is taught.*
